extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining patent subject-matter eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101, including how to identify judicial exceptions (abstract ideas, laws of nature, products of nature) and how to formulate/support rejections (Steps 2A and 2B) and responses to applicant arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature rejection explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: The rejection should identify the exception as it is recited (i.e., set forth or described) in the claim, and explain using a reasoned rationale why the product does not have markedly different characteristics from its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare the claimed product to its closest naturally occurring counterpart (the product 'in its natural state') and explain whether isolation resulted in a marked difference in structure, function, or other properties. See MPEP § 2106.04(b) for products of nature and § 2106.04(c) for the markedly different characteristics analysis. Sample explanation: specify that the claim recites X isolated from naturally occurring Y and explain why there is no indication of a marked difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain why additional elements do not add significantly more (Step 2B)
rubrics_metrics.description: After identifying the judicial exception in the rejection, identify any additional elements recited in the claim beyond the judicial exception and explain why they do not add significantly more to the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the additional elements both individually and as a combination when determining whether the claim as a whole recites eligible subject matter. Recognize that a new combination of known steps may nevertheless be patent eligible. Provide a reasoned rationale so the applicant can effectively respond. See MPEP § 2106.05 for considerations courts have found to qualify (or not) as significantly more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection only when readily apparent to examiner
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection should be made only if it is readily apparent to an examiner relying on the examiner's expertise in the art in the Step 2B inquiry that the additional elements do not amount to claiming significantly more than the recited judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, explain why the additional elements do provide an inventive concept by adding a meaningful limitation. If maintaining a rejection, provide the underlying rationale in the record. See Diamond v. Diehr and MPEP § 2106.05.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide reasoned explanation for 'well-understood, routine, conventional' findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When concluding that particular claim limitations are well-understood, routine, conventional activities (or elements) in the relevant field, the rejection should explain why the courts have recognized, or those in the relevant field would recognize, those claim limitations as such.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a reasoned explanation that supports the conventionality conclusion (do not assert conventionality without rationale). See MPEP § 2106.05(d) for more information and examples of activities/elements courts have found to be well-understood, routine, conventional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address generic computer components and functions
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that recite a generic computer component performing generic computer functions at a high level of generality, examiners can explain why these generic computing functions do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to MPEP § 2106.05(d) and § 2106.05(f) for lists/examples. Do not assume all computer functions are routine; courts have found some computer-implemented processes to be significantly more (e.g., DDR Holdings). Consider whether generic computer components in combination perform non-generic functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify insignificant extra-solution activity and field-of-use limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity (e.g., mere data gathering, final storing step) or merely link the use of the judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use, explain why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples and precedent: e.g., storing data after computing area does not add a meaningful limitation; limiting a mathematical formula to a particular industry may be insufficient (Parker v. Flook). See MPEP § 2106.05(g) and § 2106.05(h).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest claim amendments to overcome rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a best practice for the examiner to consult the specification to determine if there are elements that could be added to the claim to make it eligible, and, if so, identify those elements in the Office action and suggest them as a way to overcome the rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When appropriate, point out specification passages and possible narrowing amendments that could supply meaningful limitations or improvements to the technology to traverse a §101 rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary standard for eligibility determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: The courts consider the determination of whether a claim is eligible to be a question of law; therefore, courts generally do not require 'evidence' to identify a judicial exception and decide eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At Step 2A, a reasoned rationale identifying the judicial exception is sufficient; at Step 2B there is likewise no requirement for evidence to find lack of significantly more. However, when available, sources of evidence (e.g., specification admissions, manuals, patents, court decisions) may be provided to support assertions or rebut applicant arguments; care should be taken that cited case facts comport with the application. See cited Federal Circuit decisions (e.g., Alice, Smith, Content Extraction) and MPEP guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use prior precedent to identify exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether claimed subject matter is judicially-excepted, the Federal Circuit typically compares the claimed subject matter to subject matter identified as an exception in its prior precedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine earlier cases to see whether the claimed concept is similar to concepts previously held to be exceptions. Examples: Amdocs, In re Smith, Apple v. Ameranth, Versata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate applicant's responses and amendments fully
rubrics_metrics.description: After examiners identify and explain the reasons why a claim is directed to an exception without significantly more, the burden shifts to the applicant to amend the claim or present persuasive arguments or evidence; examiners must carefully consider all of applicant's arguments and evidence rebutting the subject matter eligibility rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant amends, determine the amended claim's broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) and reperform the eligibility analysis. If applicant persuasively establishes eligibility, withdraw the rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Considerations for what qualifies as 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: An additional element may qualify as 'significantly more' if it meaningfully limits the judicial exception, for example by improving another technology or technical field, improving the functioning of a computer itself, adding a specific limitation beyond what is well-understood/routine/conventional, or adding unconventional steps that confine the claim to a particular useful application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if an element does not amount to significantly more on its own, it can amount to significantly more when considered in combination with other elements. See MPEP § 2106.05(a), (e), (f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination of elements may amount to significantly more
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if claim elements individually are generic or conventional, their combination may enable functions that are not merely generic and therefore amount to significantly more than an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide rationale showing how the combination meaningfully limits the exception (e.g., generic computer components able in combination to perform non-generic functions). Cite DDR Holdings as an example where combination produced eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: When relying on case law, explain correspondence and avoid new grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant challenges the identification of an abstract idea that was based on a court case and the challenge is not persuasive, the examiner should explain why the abstract idea identified in the claim is similar to the concept in the cited case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the original rejection did not identify a Supreme Court or Federal Circuit decision, and applicant challenges the identification, the examiner must point to a case in which a similar abstract idea was identified and explain the correspondence to maintain the rejection. Citation to supporting case law is not a new ground unless there is a change to the basic thrust of the rejection. See MPEP § 706.07(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reevaluate conventionality when applicant rebuts with evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant responds to an examiner's assertion that something is well-known, routine, conventional activity with specific argument or evidence that the additional elements are not such, the examiner should reevaluate whether it is readily apparent that the additional elements are indeed well-known, routine, conventional activities to those who work in the relevant field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fully reevaluate the position, especially when additional elements are not discussed in the specification as known generic functions/components. If maintaining the rejection, consider whether evidence should be provided to support the rejection and clarify the record for appeal. See MPEP § 2106.05(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling 'specially programmed' or 'particular machine' amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant amends a claim to add a generic computer or generic computer components and asserts that the claim recites significantly more because the generic computer is 'specially programmed' or is a 'particular machine', the examiner should analyze whether the added elements provide significantly more than the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merely adding a generic computer, generic computer components, or a programmed computer to perform generic computer functions does not automatically overcome an eligibility rejection (see Alice and OIP Techs.). Examine whether the addition meaningfully limits the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider preemption arguments—reconsider Steps 2A and 2B
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant argues that the claim is specific and does not preempt all applications of the exception, the examiner should reconsider Step 2A to determine whether the claim is directed to an improvement to the functioning of a computer or any other technology or technical field, and if still directed to an exception, reconsider Step 2B whether the additional elements in combination amount to an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption is not a standalone test but remains an underlying concern driving the two-part framework from Alice and Mayo. Reevaluate both steps where applicant presents persuasive preemption arguments. See cited cases (Synopsys, Rapid Litigation, Ariosa).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying the record when claims are eligible or to assist applicant
rubrics_metrics.description: When the claims are deemed patent eligible, the examiner may make clarifying remarks on the record (e.g., reference the portion of the specification that describes the claimed improvement and note the claim elements that produce that improvement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarifying remarks may be made at any point during prosecution and may be useful in explaining the rationale for a rejection as well. Explaining the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) of a claim will assist applicant in understanding and responding; for example, note that a computer-readable-medium claim's BRI could cover a carrier wave and suggest narrowing amendments to overcome a rejection.
